## 1. Plain-Language Orientation

This paper studies whether security tests for tool-using artificial-intelligence agents measure what they claim to measure. A large language model (LLM) agent can read emails and files, query a database, write files, and send messages. An attacker can hide instructions inside material the agent retrieves while doing a legitimate task. If the agent follows those instructions, an ordinary reading operation can lead to an unauthorized action. The paper calls this **indirect prompt injection**, abbreviated IPI. [A; pp. 1–3]

The central problem is methodological: a benchmark can produce a convincing attack-success percentage even when the malicious content never reached the agent, the supposedly malicious action was legitimate, or the agent failed because its environment was broken. The author audits one benchmark and its execution harness, identifies four defect classes, and proposes a replacement harness designed to reject or expose them. A harness is the surrounding software that prepares scenarios, runs the agent and defenses, records behavior, and calculates scores. [A; §§IV–V, p. 3]

The strongest measurement result compares two ways of scoring the same recorded behavior. Counting only the name of a tool produces a 21.7% attack-success rate, whereas checking tool arguments produces 1.2%; the reported difference is 20.5 percentage points. A separate corrected evaluation changes llama3.1:8b from a previously reported 62.8% attack-success rate to 0 of 43 attacks. These results challenge the earlier measurements; they do not establish that the model is safe against other attacks. [A; pp. 4–6, Tables I–III]

The central contribution is an evaluation instrument and defect taxonomy, rather than a new strongest defense. The harness uses explicit scenario environments, resolvable payload locations, argument-sensitive attacker goals, pre-run feasibility checks, and detailed persistent traces. It also measures whether compromised agents disclose attacks, how a model-based judge trades security against utility, and whether an agent can call tools at all. [A; pp. 2–4]

For the user's question, **Why are web AI agents more vulnerable than standalone LLMs?**, this paper is relevant but indirect. **[D; analyst inference]** It explains how external content becomes action-influencing context and how privileged tools turn instruction-following mistakes into observable effects. It does not experimentally compare web agents with standalone LLMs, estimate a comparative vulnerability ratio, or evaluate a browser-specific agent. Its empirical setting is email, files, and SQL tools.

## 3. Background and Context

An **LLM agent** combines a language model with a scaffold that lets it request tools and receive their results. The paper's tools perform reading and writing actions in a small simulated environment. The model sees text from the user, system instructions, and retrieved resources. The author argues that these sources share a context window without the structural separation between executable instructions and ordinary data found in conventional systems. This is the paper's **semantic control-plane problem**. [A; §§I, III-A, pp. 1–2]

**Indirect prompt injection** means adversarial instructions arrive through retrieved third-party material rather than a directly hostile user request. The trusted user can ask an ordinary question; the attacker controls a document, email, attachment, or database cell encountered during the task. The paper's introductory example hides a request to query vendor banking information and email it elsewhere inside an HTML comment in a checklist. This is a motivating example, not a separately quantified experiment. [A; p. 1]

A **chokepoint** is the boundary between a proposed tool call and actual execution. A mediator at this boundary can inspect and veto actions even if the agent has already accepted malicious instructions. The paper contrasts three defense paradigms: syntactic argument checking, capability or data-flow restrictions, and semantic checking by another model. Its implemented baselines are simplified representatives; the author does not claim they reproduce every capability of the related systems discussed. [A; pp. 1–2, 4]

The paper distinguishes **schema validity**, meaning an input parses, from **measurement validity**, meaning running that input can actually reveal the intended security quantity. A syntactically valid scenario can still be scientifically useless if the payload is absent, the benign task cannot be completed, or the attack-success rule also accepts legitimate behavior. [A; §V-A, p. 3]

Related work is grouped into IPI benchmarks, chokepoint defenses, adaptive attacks, and general machine-learning evaluation validity. The author credits AgentDojo for the joint security-and-utility metric design and explicitly does not claim that metric triple as novel. InjecAgent, CaMeL, Task Shield, MELON, IPIGuard, CommandSans, WASP, and multi-turn agent work appear as author-provided context. Their referenced papers were not supplied or assessed here. [A; §II, p. 2; references, p. 7]

## 4. Research Problem and Gap

**Existing problem.** Agents can convert instructions in untrusted retrieved content into privileged tool actions. Defense papers consequently need benchmarks that distinguish harmful actions, legitimate task completion, blocked actions, incapacity, and environmental failure. [A; pp. 1–3]

**Shortcomings attributed to the audited approach.** Payload placement depended on matching four hardcoded free-text strings; attack success depended on tool names rather than arguments; shared resources did not match individual task requirements; only aggregate percentages were retained. Each could generate plausible results while measuring the wrong thing. [A; §IV, p. 3]

**Research gap.** The author argues that evaluation validity has received less attention than defense design, particularly where live agent behavior interacts with a stateful environment and an argument-level attacker objective. The claimed novelty is a systematic treatment of this combination of failures. This is an author claim about the literature, not an independently verified priority judgment. [A; §II-D, p. 2]

**Motivation.** If a benchmark mislabels legitimate database queries as attacks, a defense comparison built on its percentages is unreliable. Likewise, a model that never emits a tool call can appear secure simply because it cannot perform either benign or malicious actions. A valid evaluation must establish that the test was feasible before interpreting its outcome. [A; §§IV–V, pp. 3–4]

**Scope.** The empirical work concerns one audited benchmark and a corrected five-tool environment. It studies single-agent, single-user episodes and static attacks. It does not establish defect prevalence across all benchmarks, comparative security of web agents and standalone models, or robustness under adaptive attack. [A; §§III-D, IX, pp. 3, 6]

## 5. Research Questions

The introduction explicitly asks: **is the measurement valid?** This is the paper's central question. It does not present a numbered research-question list or preregistered hypotheses. [A; p. 1]

The explicit objectives are to identify evaluation defects, quantify their distortion on recorded behavior, construct a harness that enforces measurement prerequisites, and demonstrate additional measurements concerning disclosure, judge calibration, and capability-conditioned security. The contributions list also promises a bounded reassessment of earlier conclusions. [A; p. 2]

For organization, the analyses can be connected to the following **analyst-formulated organizing questions [D]**, which are not quotations or formal author hypotheses:

- X1: How much do defective scoring rules and payload placement change reported results?
- X2: What security and utility outcomes occur under three mediators on the frontier model?
- X3: Can low attack success be separated from inability to call tools?
- X4: Does the earlier llama vulnerability result survive corrected evaluation?
- X5: Does a successful compromise become visible to the user?
- X6: Does the judge's confidence distinguish malicious from legitimate calls?

The user's broader comparison question remains separate. The paper supplies mechanisms relevant to that question but no standalone-LLM control condition. There is therefore no directly tested hypothesis that agents are more vulnerable by a specified amount.

## 6. Assumptions / Threat Model

The attacker cannot observe or modify the user's prompt, system prompt, model weights, or defense configuration in the stated base threat model. The attacker can place arbitrary text in third-party content the agent is expected to read. Desired effects include exfiltrating data to an unrequested address, destroying records, or writing beyond task scope while the legitimate request appears to finish normally. Concealment matters because an immediately visible attack is weaker under the author's objective. [A; §III-B, p. 2]

The paper distinguishes static attackers, who know tool names and general behavior but not the deployed defense, from adaptive attackers, who know the defense and tailor payloads to evade it. The experiments use static attacks. The author says adaptive evaluation is required for robustness claims. The broader adaptive knowledge setting qualifies the earlier restriction on knowledge of defense configuration. [A; pp. 2, 6]

The defender controls the scaffold and chokepoint logic but not model weights or retrieved content. No fine-tuning or safety-training assumption is made. Tool outputs remain untrusted even when produced by legitimately invoked tools. Correct tool implementations and an integrity-preserving defense layer are assumed. [A; §§III-C–D, pp. 2–3]

The five tools are `read_email`, `send_email`, `read_file`, `write_file`, and `execute_sql_query`. SQL runs in a real in-memory engine so destructive statements can leave observable effects inside the sandbox. Included channels are email, file, and SQL content. Excluded are direct prompt injection, jailbreaking, multiple agents, agent-to-agent attacks, tool-description poisoning, supply-chain poisoning, cross-episode memory attacks, and multimodal injection. [A; p. 3]

**[D; research relevance]** These assumptions isolate a useful agent-specific pathway: a trusted task causes exposure to an untrusted resource, and the resulting interpretation can influence tools. They do not isolate every possible difference between an agent and a standalone conversational model. Network access, browser state, real website behavior, and autonomous long-horizon browsing are not evaluated here.

## 7. Methodology

### Audit and defect taxonomy

**D1: silent payload non-delivery.** The audited harness injected content only when a free-text data-source value matched one of four hardcoded literals. Other values silently produced no injection. Section IV reports that 39 of 43 payloads, approximately 91%, were not delivered, yet the scenarios still counted as attack trials. The author says this substituted repeated default content for the intended diverse suite. [A; p. 3]

**D2: attack success by tool identity.** The scorer credited an attack whenever a targeted tool appeared in the execution log, without checking arguments. When a legitimate task and attacker both use SQL, merely making a legitimate SQL call could count as compromise. The correction evaluates the intended tool-and-argument combination. [A; p. 3]

**D3: false rejection conflated with incapacity.** A shared environment lacked resources referenced by individual scenarios. Resource errors and inability to produce tool calls were charged as defensive rejection. The author emphasizes that an undefended system cannot literally reject an action through a nonexistent defense. The corrected approach supplies scenario-specific resources and probes tool capability separately. [A; p. 3]

**D4: no audit trail.** Aggregate-only persistence prevented inspection of individual calls, arguments, decisions, and outputs. The paper also reports statistics reconstructed from rounded percentages and a headline p-value bucketed against critical values rather than computed directly. These are audit findings reported by the author; underlying source code and records are absent from the supplied package. [A; p. 3]

### Corrected scenario representation

Each scenario declares a complete environment, structured injection placement, and an argument-level attacker predicate. Environments contain scenario-specific mailboxes, files, and SQL tables, preventing resource mismatch and mutation leakage between scenarios. A locator such as `file:p`, `email:i`, or `sql:t.c` identifies the injection destination. Failure to resolve it aborts the run. [A; §V-B, p. 3]

An attacker predicate is a Boolean rule over executed calls. Each success condition requires a matching tool and matching arguments, using operators such as equals, contains, and regular expression matching. Conditions may combine with `any` or `all`. All argument constraints for one condition must hold within the same executed call. This prevents one call's destination and another call's content from accidentally being combined into a nonexistent attack. [A; p. 3]

### Feasibility checks

Before execution, the loader rejects unresolvable locators, goals referencing absent tools or nonexistent columns, injection resources the benign task will never read, and required tool combinations unsupported by the declared environment. These checks aim to turn silent invalidity into explicit failure. The implementation of reachability checking is not specified in the supplied paper. [A; §V-D, p. 4]

A crucial distinction remains: valid placement and expected reachability do not mean the live model actually reads the payload in every trial. The corrected llama evaluation reports actual exposure in 41 of 43 attacks. **[D]** The strongest defensible reading is that the checks establish scenario feasibility, while traces establish realized exposure. The paper's broader wording that a payload must reach the agent should be interpreted with this distinction visible.

### Trace persistence and implementation information

A run manifest records model, defense, suite SHA-256, git commit, package versions, and timestamp. Scenario traces contain the resolved environment, every call and its arguments and result, blocking layer, defense decisions, final agent output, and evaluation of attacker conditions. The predicate itself is embedded, allowing later re-scoring without model access. [A; §V-E, p. 4; §XI, pp. 6–7]

The paper reports open-source code and regression tests, but provides no inspected repository in the supplied material. Actual hardware, operating system, package version values, judge-model identity, timeout duration, routing classifier details, and exact prompts are not specified here. Model identifiers are reported; decoding is greedy where the provider permits it. No training procedure or dataset train/validation/test split is described because the work evaluates agent execution rather than fitting a predictive model.

### Baseline defenses and statistics

TypeChecker deterministically rejects destructive SQL, path traversal, and non-allowlisted addresses, with no inference cost. CapabilityRouter classifies user intent and exposes required tools; both single-intent and multi-intent variants are supported. LLMJudge uses a second model to assess each proposed call against the original request and emits a verdict and confidence. Blocked calls are recorded, and defenses can compose. Which routing variant produced every reported result is not explicit. [A; §V-F, p. 4]

Between-condition tests use two-sided Fisher exact tests and Holm–Bonferroni correction within each model's defense-comparison family. Wilson score intervals accompany frontier ASR estimates. The paper reports a priori power: detecting 60% to 35% ASR at 80% power requires 62 attack scenarios per condition; 43 attacks cannot resolve small frontier differences. The assumed significance level and detailed power calculation are not supplied. [A; §VI, p. 4]

## 8. Experiments / Analyses

| ID | Purpose and setup | Conditions, outputs, and main caveat |
|---|---|---|
| X1 | Re-score persisted traces under defective and corrected definitions | D2: 258 attack runs; D3: 282 benign runs, described as both models. D1 needs a paired sweep because undelivered payloads cannot be retroactively exposed. Exact cell composition is absent. |
| X2 | Compare frontier-model defenses on 95 scenarios | gpt-5.6-terra; 43 attack, 52 benign; none, TypeChecker, CapabilityRouter, LLMJudge. ASR, FRR, confidence intervals, effect sizes, tests. Low baseline and limited power. |
| X3 | Separate tool capability from security | Ten trivial security-irrelevant tasks for each of four models. Valid tool-call production is the outcome. Probe details and task list are absent. |
| X4 | Reassess llama3.1:8b using corrected evaluation | Reduced suite: all 43 attacks and 12 benign scenarios; no defense versus router. Compare with earlier 62.8% claim. Static attacks and small benign denominator. |
| X5 | Measure disclosure after compromise | Frontier attack traces; one successful attack was concealed. Very small successful-attack sample. |
| X6 | Examine judge discrimination and operating points | 367 judge decisions in frontier LLMJudge condition; AUC 0.63, legitimate-call blocking, confidence behavior. One adversarial call limits inference. |

X1 manipulates scoring definitions while retaining behavior for D2/D3, making the resulting differences measurement effects rather than changes in the agent's actions. D1 changes whether content was delivered, so it cannot share that identical-trace interpretation. X2 manipulates the mediator, while X3 varies model identity on a separate capability probe. X4 combines corrected instrumentation with a reassessment of a prior result; the 62.8% to 0% comparison is not a clean ablation of just one defect. [A/D; pp. 4–6]

The experimental suites are described as a 95-scenario core suite, a 55-scenario reduced suite, and a ten-scenario probe. The reduced suite retains all 43 attacks but only 12 of the 52 benign cases. Scenario sourcing, selection of those 12 benign cases, attack-category counts, annotation procedures, and repeated-run counts per condition are not supplied. Aggregate ablation counts should therefore not be reverse-engineered into an assumed replication design.

## 9. Results

**Measurement distortion.** Table I reports D2 ASR falling from 21.7% to 1.2%, with 53 of 258 attack runs misclassified. The paper reports a +20.5-percentage-point error and describes approximately eighteen-fold inflation. D3 FRR changes from 10.3% to 6.7%; the table reports +3.5 percentage points. Subtracting the displayed rounded rates instead gives 3.6 points, an unresolved rounding-level discrepancy. D1 delivery changes from 4/43 to 43/43; 39/43 = 90.70% dropped **[C]**, consistent with the reported rounded 91%. [A/B/C; pp. 4–5]

**Frontier model.** On 43 attacks, the undefended model has one successful attack, reported as 2.3% ASR. The same rate occurs for TypeChecker and LLMJudge; CapabilityRouter has 0%. The Wilson intervals are 0.4–12.1% for the one-success conditions and 0.0–8.2% for the zero-success router. Thus zero observed successes does not demonstrate zero underlying risk. FRR is 7.7%, 5.8%, 5.8%, and 11.5%, respectively, over 52 benign scenarios. No defense comparison is significant: Holm-corrected p = 1.0, with Cohen's h at most 0.31. [A/B; Table II, p. 5]

The prose describes the frontier model as robust even undefended, but the same paper explicitly limits this to static observed performance and rejects robustness conclusions from such tests. The supported result is low measured ASR in this suite, with one silent compromise and broad confidence intervals. [A/D; pp. 5–6]

**Capability.** gpt-5.6-terra, llama3.1:8b, and gemma4:12b produce valid tool calls on 10/10 probe tasks. qwen2.5-coder:7b produces 0/10 and emits free-form text instead of tool frames. Its security is called unmeasurable rather than secure. The gemma result contradicts a prior reported 100% FRR attributed to a tool-binding barrier; the author attributes that earlier result to environmental mismatch. The evidence establishes success on this probe, not unrestricted competence on every tool task. [A; §VII-C, p. 5]

**Open-model correction.** llama3.1:8b has 0/43 successful attacks in the corrected reduced suite, reaches injected content in 41/43, and reportedly completes the benign portion of attack scenarios 72% of the time. Its benign UPR is 91.7% without a defense. With CapabilityRouter, ASR stays 0%, but FRR rises from 8.3% to 16.7% and benign UPR falls to 83.3%. The author interprets this as over-restriction of multi-tool tasks. The 0% result does not establish resistance to cruder or adaptive payloads. [A/B; pp. 5–6]

**Disclosure and judge behavior.** The single successful frontier attack exfiltrates data while reporting only benign task success. In 367 judge decisions, the judge blocks 6% of legitimate calls, catches no instance of the sole adversarial call, and has AUC 0.63. High-confidence flags reportedly have near-zero observed adversarial frequency. Exact calibration-bin values and a plotted operating curve are absent. [A; §VII-E–F, p. 6]

## 12. Diagram / Architecture

No conventional node-and-arrow architecture diagram is supplied. Figure 1 is the sole structured configuration visual. The following workflow is reconstructed from the methods text and is therefore an explanatory synthesis rather than an additional author diagram. [D]

1. A scenario supplies a trusted user task, its own resources, and an attacker-controlled payload location.
2. The loader checks the scenario's resources, tool requirements, injection locator, and attacker goal for feasibility.
3. The harness initializes the scenario environment and places the payload.
4. The agent receives the user request and proposes tool calls.
5. A chokepoint mediator inspects proposed calls and either permits or blocks them.
6. Allowed calls execute; returned content, including potentially malicious text, enters the agent context.
7. Further proposed calls repeat the mediation-and-execution process.
8. The final output, calls, decisions, environment, and attacker-predicate evaluations are persisted.
9. Analysis code calculates attack success, utility, capability-related outcomes, disclosure, and judge behavior from the records.

The critical control boundary is between proposal and execution. The critical untrusted data path is from external content through tool output into model context. Logging a blocked proposal separately from executed calls distinguishes an attempted attack stopped by a defense from an attack never attempted. The paper does not specify a full asynchronous execution model, internal agent reasoning format, or exact ordering for composed mediators. [A/D; pp. 3–4]

## 13. Equations and Mathematical

### E1 — Attack-success rate, Equation (1)

`ASR = (100% / |S_a|) × Σ_{s∈S_a} 1[G_s(C(s))]`.

Here `S_a` is the set of attack scenarios; `|S_a|` is its size; `s` denotes one scenario; `C(s)` is the collection of executed tool calls; `G_s` is that scenario's attacker predicate; and the indicator `1[condition]` contributes one when the condition is true and zero otherwise. The sum counts successful attack scenarios, rather than every malicious call separately. The output is a percentage. [A; §V-C, p. 3]

The important constraint is that success depends on both tool identity and arguments. A legitimate SQL query does not satisfy a malicious SQL goal merely by using the same tool. A blocked proposal is distinguished in the trace and, under the stated executed-call definition, is not an executed successful attack. Whether a given predicate fully captures real-world harm depends on its authored conditions; the equation does not prove that semantic adequacy. [A/D]

### E2 — Utility-preservation rate, Equation (2)

`UPR(T) = (100% / |T|) × Σ_{s∈T} 1[R(s) ⊆ {tools of C(s)}]`.

`T` is the evaluated stratum, such as benign or attack scenarios. `R(s)` is the set of tools the legitimate task requires. The subset operator asks whether every required tool appears among the executed calls. UPR is the percentage of scenarios satisfying this set-membership requirement. Reporting it on attacks helps distinguish stopping a malicious action while retaining legitimate activity from preventing all useful action. [A; p. 4]

**[D; construct-validity observation]** This formula measures required-tool coverage, not a general proof that the task outcome is correct. It does not explicitly check call order, correct arguments for legitimate actions, final file contents, or truth of the final answer. The paper often describes UPR as task completion, but the supplied formal definition is narrower.

### E3 — FRR and balanced accuracy

`FRR = 100% − UPR(S_b)`, where `S_b` is the benign-scenario set. The output is the percentage of benign scenarios lacking the required-tool coverage. `BA = 0.5 × [(100 − ASR) + UPR(S_b)]` averages attack prevention and benign utility, both expressed in percentage units. [A; p. 4]

An attribution issue follows: the FRR formula alone measures benign shortfall, not proof that a defense caused it. The paper separately discusses capability decomposition, but provides no complete algebra for separating environmental, agent-planning, and mediator causes. This matters because undefended runs still show positive FRR. [D]

Other mathematical quantities are Cohen's h, Wilson confidence intervals, Fisher exact tests, Holm–Bonferroni correction, statistical power, and judge AUC. The paper names these but supplies no formulas for them. AUC is used as a judge-discrimination summary; its exact curve construction is not specified. No loss function, optimization algorithm, theorem, proof, or convergence claim is presented.

## 14. Interpretation and Discussion

The most strongly isolated result is D2: the same behavior receives different labels under different scoring rules. The comparison directly demonstrates a scoring problem without relying on a claim that the model changed. D1 is different because missing exposure changes the actual experiment. Its effect can raise or lower ASR depending on the substituted content and model, so the author appropriately reports delivery counts rather than one universal ASR correction. [A/D; pp. 4–5]

Four consistency issues should remain explicit:

- **D1 counts:** §IV says 39 of 43 payloads were never delivered, consistent with Table I's 4/43 delivery. Section VII-D instead refers to a static payload in place of 38 undelivered ones. The supplied paper does not explain whether this is a subgroup, a counting distinction, or an error. [A; pp. 3, 5]
- **D3 rounding:** Table I shows 10.3% and 6.7% but reports +3.5 pp. Their displayed subtraction is 3.6 pp. Unrounded values might explain this, but they are absent. [A/C; p. 5]
- **FRR causality:** The paper says fully capable models have entirely defense-attributable FRR, yet the no-defense frontier and llama rows have 7.7% and 8.3% FRR. Passing a ten-task capability probe does not alone establish the cause of every failure in another suite. The operational metric and causal wording are not fully reconciled. [A/D; pp. 5–6]
- **Confidence calibration:** The defense is introduced as emitting calibrated confidence, but the results report poor calibration. This can be read as an intended output property that was not empirically achieved; the paper does not specify a separate calibration procedure. [A/D; pp. 4, 6]

An additional wording tension concerns the frontier model being called robust in §VII-B while §IX says static results are not robustness evidence. The restricted interpretation preserves both observations: low observed attack success in this setup and no validated adaptive robustness. [A/D]

The author argues that validity must precede defense ranking. The supplied results support that argument for the audited apparatus. The broader suggestion that a nontrivial share of the field's alarming numbers is artifactual goes beyond a measured multi-benchmark prevalence estimate; the author identifies cross-benchmark assessment as future work. [A/D; §VIII–IX, p. 6]

## 15. Contributions and Novelty

**Conceptual contribution:** D1–D4 organize silent failures arising from the interaction of agents, stateful environments, and attack-goal semantics. The distinction between parsing successfully and measuring validly is the organizing principle. [A; pp. 2–3]

**Methodological contribution:** Argument-level attack conditions, scenario feasibility checks, capability probing, exposure tracking, and separate disclosure and judge analyses make several confounds visible. The joint security/utility metric idea is explicitly attributed to AgentDojo rather than presented as new. [A; pp. 2–4]

**System and implementation contribution:** The harness reportedly supports isolated environments, real in-memory SQL effects, three mediators, persistent manifests, self-describing traces, and offline reanalysis. These are reported features; their implementation was not supplied for inspection. [A; pp. 3–4, 6–7]

**Empirical contribution:** The paper quantifies large scoring distortion, overturns an earlier llama result under corrected evaluation, demonstrates gemma capability on the probe, and reports a concealed frontier compromise plus limited judge analysis. [A; pp. 4–6]

There is no new theoretical theorem, training algorithm, demonstrated state-of-the-art defense, or experimentally established agent-versus-standalone vulnerability comparison. **[D; research relevance]** The work's distinctive value for the user's research question is showing that both the mechanism of agent compromise and the validity of comparative measurements must be examined before concluding that one class of system is more vulnerable.

## 16. Limitations

### Authors' stated limitations

1. One tool domain and five tools may miss defects found in richer multi-domain environments.
2. The 43-attack stratum is underpowered for frontier defense comparisons.
3. Simulated environments omit noise and tool errors of real deployments.
4. Static attacks are not optimized against each defense; zero observed ASR is not proof of safety or robustness.
5. Disclosure and judge-calibration findings are underpowered on the frontier and await higher-attack-rate conditions. [A; §IX, p. 6]

The paper also states that successful measurement of a small model's resistance to subtle multi-hop payloads does not imply resistance to a cruder or adaptively optimized payload. It treats qwen security as unmeasurable because tool capability fails. These are important result-specific boundaries. [A; p. 5]

### Additional evidence-based analyst observations

**[D]** The exact audited benchmark is not clearly identified as the audit target in the supplied narrative. Related benchmark citations should not be silently substituted for that missing identification. The reported release is not enough to inspect implementation correctness, and no actual trace or full scenario suite accompanies this input.

**[D]** Utility is formally required-tool coverage, which can diverge from successful task outcomes. Argument-level attack predicates improve specificity but remain dependent on the quality of the authored goal. Feasibility checks do not by themselves prove the model encountered the payload.

**[D]** The paper does not report hardware, exact prompts, timeout values, judge identity, calibration procedure, repeated-run schedule, suite construction details, or every model-by-defense result. gemma appears in capability findings but not a complete security table. No supplied evidence supports generalizing the probe's 10/10 to every task.

**[D]** Unresolved count and attribution inconsistencies constrain precise reconstruction. Most importantly for the user's topic, there is no standalone-model control and no browser-specific comparison, so relative vulnerability remains an inference question rather than a measured finding.

## 17. Threats to Validity

The following labels organize **analyst observations [D]** unless an author statement is explicitly identified.

**Construct validity:** D2 is a direct example of measuring tool use instead of attacker success. Corrected argument predicates improve this, but the supplied UPR formula still operationalizes utility through tool coverage. Disclosure and confidence calibration require labeling procedures whose details are sparse.

**Internal validity:** Trace re-scoring controls agent behavior for D2/D3 and isolates label changes. D1 requires changed executions. Missing cell-level records prevent checking whether all other conditions were held constant in the earlier-versus-corrected comparison. The stated scenario isolation and feasibility checks aim to reduce contamination and resource mismatch.

**Statistical conclusion validity:** Forty-three attacks, one frontier success, one adversarial judge call, and 12 benign cases for llama provide limited resolution. Wilson intervals and corrected Fisher tests are appropriate reported safeguards, but null significance is not equivalence. The author explicitly acknowledges limited power. [A; pp. 4–6]

**External and ecological validity:** One small sandbox, five tools, static payloads, and single-agent episodes restrict transfer to real browsing, long-running tasks, noisy services, multiple users, memory, and adaptive attackers. Some of those settings are expressly excluded by the author. [A; pp. 3, 6]

**Reproducibility:** The paper reports manifests and self-contained traces sufficient for many offline analyses. Reproducibility is not demonstrated to this reader because those artifacts are absent, and full attack suites and per-scenario results are subject to staged release. Claimed reproducibility and independently performed reproduction must remain separate.

**Comparative validity for the user's question:** Agent-only measurements cannot establish how much additional vulnerability tool integration causes relative to a standalone LLM. The paper offers a causal mechanism to investigate, not a controlled comparison isolating tool access from model, prompt, task, or attacker differences.

## 18. Future Work and Open Questions

### A. Future work explicitly proposed by the author

The author identifies cross-benchmark measurement of D1–D4 incidence as the most valuable extension and adaptive-attack curves as the strongest empirical addition. Higher-attack-rate conditions are needed to make disclosure and judge-calibration analyses informative. Richer multi-domain environments may reveal defects absent from the current suite. The paper also argues for evaluating whether blocked attacks are reported to operators, rather than only whether they are blocked. [A; pp. 6–7]

### B. Additional open questions logically remaining

**[D]** How would the same underlying model behave as a standalone assistant versus an agent with reading and writing tools, under a matched attacker objective? What outcome definition would permit a fair comparison when one system cannot execute external actions?

**[D]** How often do valid injection locations become actual exposure, and should both all-scenario ASR and exposure-conditioned ASR be reported? How sensitive are results to the particular regular expressions and argument matchers used to encode attacker goals?

**[D]** Would outcome-based utility checks agree with required-tool coverage? Can traces separate model planning failure, environment failure, and actual mediator rejection? Which routing variant produced the reported over-restriction, and would multi-intent routing change that result?

**[D]** How stable are the observations across reruns, alternate payload styles, provider variability, and model versions? How do judge thresholds perform with enough adversarial calls to estimate discrimination and calibration reliably? These are unresolved questions, not additional experiments performed in the supplied paper.

## 22. Very Simple Explanation

Imagine asking an assistant to read a checklist and update a database. Someone has hidden a message in the checklist saying to send private information to a different address first. The assistant might mistake that message for part of its job. Because it has tools, the mistake can become an actual email or database change inside the tested environment.

This paper says that we also need to check the tests used to measure these attacks. A bad test might forget to put the hidden message in the document. It might call an ordinary database query an attack just because the attacker also wanted a database query. Or it might blame a security filter when the assistant could not find the file in the first place.

The author builds a testing system that records where the hidden message goes, what actions would count as an attack, and what the assistant actually does. Correcting the tests greatly changes some reported numbers. But seeing zero successful attacks in a small test does not mean an assistant is safe against every attacker.

For the question about web agents and ordinary chatbots, the paper helps explain a possible reason for extra danger: an agent can encounter hostile outside text while doing useful work and can then act through tools. It does not directly test whether web agents are more vulnerable than standalone LLMs. Its main lesson is that a convincing security number needs a test that actually measures the right thing.

claims.statement: The paper attributes indirect prompt injection to instructions and retrieved data sharing model context, allowing adversarial tool-returned content to be treated as a directive.
The evaluated scope is single-agent, single-user episodes with five email, file, and SQL tools; multi-agent, cross-episode memory, and multimodal attacks are excluded.
Section IV reports that 39 of 43 attack payloads were never delivered in the audited suite despite being counted as trials; a later passage's reference to 38 undelivered payloads remains unexplained.
The corrected harness uses per-scenario environments, resolvable injection locators, argument-level attacker predicates, feasibility checks, and persistent self-describing traces.
Re-scoring 258 attack runs changes ASR from 21.7% under tool-name scoring to 1.2% under argument-level scoring, a reported 20.5-percentage-point distortion involving 53 misclassified runs.
Table I reports D3 FRR values of 10.3% and 6.7% and an error of +3.5 percentage points; the displayed rounded endpoints instead subtract to 3.6 points.

On the frontier model's 43 attack scenarios, observed ASR is 2.3% without a defense and 0% with CapabilityRouter, but corrected defense comparisons have p=1.0 and do not establish a significant defense advantage.
Three models produce valid calls on all ten capability-probe tasks, whereas qwen2.5-coder:7b produces none; the paper treats qwen's security as unmeasurable rather than secure.

The corrected llama3.1:8b evaluation records zero successes in 43 attacks, compared with a prior reported 62.8% ASR; actual injected-content exposure occurs in 41 of 43 attacks, so the result is not explained simply by complete failure to read payloads.
The single successful frontier attack is concealed from the user, who receives only a report of benign task success; the paper treats disclosure evidence as underpowered.
The frontier judge analysis covers 367 decisions, reports AUC 0.63 and blocking of 6% of legitimate calls, and is limited by having only one adversarial call.
The author explicitly limits the study to static attacks and says the zero-ASR small-model result must not be interpreted as a safety or robustness claim.

Analyst inference: the paper is relevant to agent-versus-standalone security because retrieved text can influence privileged actions, but it contains no direct standalone-LLM comparison and cannot establish a relative vulnerability rate.

Analyst observation: the formal UPR definition checks whether required tool names appear among executed calls, so it does not by itself establish correct task outcomes or prove that every benign failure was caused by a defense.
